newsitem.title: ITALY: Italy's Prodi meets farmers on milk quota dispute.
newsitem.headline: Italy's Prodi meets farmers on milk quota dispute.

text.p: An Italian farmers' group said on Wednesday that Prime Minister Romano Prodi had prepared a package of financial incentives for dairy farmers who faces big fines for exceeding European Union milk quotas.
Sante Ricci, president of the Confederation of Agricultural Producers, said the incentives included low-interest loans and compensation for selling cows as a way to reduce milk output.

Prodi scheduled a series of meetings with farm sector officials on Wednesday to quell increasing anger among dairy farmers over a so-called super-levy of 190 million Ecus ($225 million) for overproducing milk by some 400,000 tonnes on a national quota of 9.9 million tonnes.
Prodi, who has said the government cannot pay the fines as some of the farmers have demanded, earlier on Wednesday had been briefed on the situation by Agriculture Minister Michele Pinto.
Pinto had returned the day before from Brussels where he had sought an increase of about 6,000 tonnes in Italy's milk quota.
EU officials said the request would have to be looked at in a broader context as other members might seek higher quotas too.
As Pinto briefed Prodi at a cabinet meeting, several dozen dairy farmers from the Lazio region surrounding Rome demonstrated in the square outside the prime minister's office.
"The government will do what it can to ease the big problems in the sector, but it has to act within the limits of the law," Prodi told a news conference after the cabinet meeting.
The protesters had scattered by the time Prodi began his round of afternoon meetings.
Ricci, who was the first to meet Prodi, told reporters the prime minister told him he planned to present the incentive package in a decree law. He did not say when it would be ready.

Asked what his response was to Prodi's proposal, Ricci said he asked that the fines, which are due to be paid by January 31, be frozen until a full accounting could be done to determine exactly how much individual farmers have to pay.
The farmers say they are victims of tough EU quotas dating from the 1980s, which let them produce less than 60 percent of Italy's milk needs. The rest is imported from within the EU. ($1=.8425 Ecu)
